title: A Universal Control Budget for First-Passage Kinetics
abstract: The first-passage time is the natural observable of reaction completion, yet how its mean responds to a rate change has lacked a general constraint. We show that the logarithmic sensitivity of the mean first-passage time of any finite Markov chain to any rate is bounded by one in magnitude, and that these sensitivities sum to -1. Together the two laws form a conserved control budget: speeding completion through some transitions must be paid for by others, and a coordinated change shifts the completion time only as far as the budget allows. Raising an activation barrier or shifting the depth of a well moves many rates at once, yet neither can shift the completion time further than a single rate could. The budget caps kinetic-proofreading discrimination at the checkpoint count, and prices it in sensitivity to substrate concentration.
summary: The paper derives a 'Universal Control Budget' that constrains how the mean first-passage time of any Markov process can be controlled by changing reaction rates. It shows that speeding up completion via some reactions must be compensated by slowing down others, establishing fundamental limits on kinetic control mechanisms like molecular discrimination.
main_problem: To establish a general, universal constraint—a 'control budget'—governing how the mean first-passage time (MFPT) of any finite Markov chain responds to changes in its microscopic reaction rates.
main_result: The sensitivities of the MFPT with respect to individual rates are governed by two laws: a local unit bound ($|s_e| \le 1$) and a global summation rule ($\sum s_e = -1$), forming a conserved control budget that dictates how rate changes must be compensated.
method: The analysis maps the transient first-passage problem to an equivalent steady-state current, allowing the application of established response theory for Markov jump processes to derive sensitivity identities and bounds.
model_or_system: The model is a continuous-time Markov jump process on a finite state space with a source state (A) and an absorbing target state (B). Applications include kinetic proofreading mechanisms like T-cell antigen recognition.
key_observables: Mean First-Passage Time ($	au_{A	o B}$), Rate Sensitivities ($s_e$), Speeding/Delaying Budgets ($\mathbf{B}_+, \mathbf{B}_-$), and Discrimination Gain ($\Delta$).
important_parameters: The checkpoint count, substrate concentration sensitivity, and the ratio of forward to reset rates in proofreading.
main_assumptions: The system is modeled as a finite Markov chain with positive rates; the analysis relies on mapping $	au_{A	o B}$ to the reciprocal of a stationary current ($	ilde{j}_{A	o B}$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two response laws (local bound and global sum) using simple chains, demonstrate the mathematical 'redirection' from transient to steady-state currents, and show budget spending in kinetic proofreading.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general sensitivity framework by deriving the local and global summation rules. It then applies this budget concept to specific physical scenarios, notably analyzing how discrimination gain ($\Delta$) in kinetic proofreading is constrained by these universal bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful mathematical constraint on non-equilibrium dynamics, which is highly relevant for understanding rate control in complex biological or chemical systems modeled by master equations.
